Analysis: Both hypotheses are innovative. Hypothesis 1 leverages nanoparticle delivery and pH-triggered conversion of EGCG from an antioxidant to a prooxidant, targeting CSCs by inducing mitochondrial oxidative stress and inhibiting IL-8 signaling. This approach is novel but faces challenges in mechanistic clarity, ensuring specificity due to CSC heterogeneity, and managing potential off‐target toxicity from the nanoparticle system. Hypothesis 2 targets CSCs by exploiting their unique mitochondrial vulnerabilities to impair oxidative phosphorylation and simultaneously modulate IL-8 and PI3K/AKT pathways, leading to energy depletion and apoptosis. It is also novel but builds on established bioenergetic distinctions and integrates advanced technologies (e.g., high-resolution respirometry, single-cell metabolomics) that enhance testability. In terms of plausibility, Hypothesis 2 has a more straightforward mechanistic rationale focused on metabolic stress, whereas Hypothesis 1’s reliance on a precise pH-triggered conversion and nanoparticle targeting adds complexity. Regarding testability, Hypothesis 2’s clear endpoints and advanced analytical techniques offer a more robust experimental framework. Finally, Hypothesis 2 appears relatively safer because it avoids the additional risks associated with nanoparticle delivery systems. Overall, Hypothesis 2 scores higher on plausibility, testability, and safety while maintaining strong novelty.
